claims.claim: the vernal-pool breeders are the wood frog and the spotted and blue-spotted salamanders
claims.source_value: blue-spotted salamanders, spotted salamanders and wood frogs breed almost exclusively in vernal pools
claims.location: web page (one page), 2nd paragraph of the post
claims.quote: blue-spotted salamanders, spotted salamanders, and wood frogs breed almost exclusively in vernal pools
claims.conditions: Maine, general statement in a popular agency blog post

claims.claim: they migrate on warm rainy nights, above about 4–7 °C
claims.source_value: mass migrations are often triggered on rainy nights once the ground is thawed and night temperatures stay above 40 degrees (°F implied: 4.4 °C); no upper figure, and 'warm' is not the post's word
claims.location: web page (one page), 3rd paragraph of the post
claims.quote: rainy nights once the ground is thawed, and nighttime temperatures remain above 40 degrees
claims.conditions: Maine; night temperature; rain and thawed ground are both part of the trigger
claims.note: From this post the paper can say 'on rainy nights with thawed ground, when night temperatures stay above about 4 °C (40 °F)'. The '4–7 °C' range is the project note's widening of 40 °F with other sources it cites beside the blog (Portland Press Herald 2026; Maine Coast Heritage Trust), not checked here.

claims.claim: migration begins in mid-March in southern Maine
claims.source_value: in some years southern and central Maine have 'big night' conditions as early as March (no day of the month)
claims.location: web page (one page), 3rd paragraph of the post
claims.quote: Southern and Central Maine experience these “big night” conditions as early as March
claims.conditions: 'Some years'; southern and central Maine together
claims.note: The post supports a March start only loosely ('as early as March', some years, southern and central Maine). The 'mid-March' wording is Calhoun & deMaynadier 2001's (cited beside the blog; not checked here).

claims.claim: migration runs to mid-May in the north of Maine
claims.note: The post gives no end date and nothing on northern Maine's timing. The mid-March (south) to mid-May (north) range belongs to Calhoun & deMaynadier 2001, the other source in the citation.

claims.claim: fish make lakeshores 'biological sinks' for spotted salamanders
claims.note: The post says vernal pools draw amphibians because they cannot hold fish ('a nearly predator-free oasis') but says nothing of lakeshores or sinks. The quoted phrase is Calhoun & deMaynadier 2001's.

notes: A short popular post (8 April 2022). It supports three things in §3.8.6: the three obligate vernal-pool breeders, the trigger (rainy nights, thawed ground, nights above 40 °F) and a start 'as early as March' in southern and central Maine in some years. The mid-March to mid-May range and 'biological sinks' belong to Calhoun & deMaynadier 2001, so the citation should split: '(Kintz 2022)' after the trigger sentence, '(Calhoun & deMaynadier 2001)' after the timing and sinks. The '4–7 °C' should become 'about 4 °C (40 °F)' unless another source gives 7 °C. Other content: more than half of Maine's amphibians and reptiles visit vernal pools at some point; MARAP counts 36 species of reptiles and amphibians in Maine; breeding adults are often faithful to the pools where they were born; Maine Big Night volunteers help amphibians across roads. The post gives no eastern-Maine dates. No code cites it. show.mjs matched every 'MDIFW n.d.' in §3.8 to this key; only the §3.8.6 sentence (03_synthesis_fish_to_forest.md:1240–1242, 'MDIFW n.d., amphibian blog') cites this post. The other 'MDIFW n.d.' citations there are the other MDIFW_nd-* entries.
